artiest/mongezi-feza.text:
Mongezi Feza (1945 to 1975) was a South African jazz trumpeter, flautist and composer. He was born in Queenstown in the Cape Province, into a family of musicians. His older brother Sandi taught him to play the trumpet in the township of Mlungisi. He received his first trumpet at the age of eight. In 1962 he joined Chris McGregor's Blue Notes, who were named best band at a South African jazz festival in 1963 but, because of the apartheid laws, could hardly perform together.

In 1964 Feza left South Africa with the Blue Notes. They played first in France and Switzerland and then settled in London, where Feza also lived in Copenhagen. When the group broke up at the end of the 1960s, he played in McGregor's sextet and in his Brotherhood of Breath, with Dudu Pukwana, Johnny Dyani and the Afro-rock group Assagai, and with rock musicians such as Robert Wyatt, Henry Cow, Centipede and Gary Windo.

Feza was influenced by the hard bop player Clifford Brown and by Don Cherry, the leading figure of free jazz. His playing combined hard bop, free jazz and jazz rock. His compositions Sonia and You Ain't Gonna Know Me ('Cos You Think You Know Me) remained in the repertoire of his colleagues for a long time. He died in London in December 1975 of untreated pneumonia. Shortly afterwards his old bandmates recorded Blue Notes for Mongezi in his memory. His own recordings appeared on, among others, Music For Xaba.
artiest/mongezi-feza.listen: Listen to a track from Music For Xaba and notice how sharp and singing the trumpet sounds, and how the music shifts from free to structured and back again.

artiest/mongo-santamaria.text:
Ramón Mongo Santamaría was born in Havana in 1917. As a child he learned to play the conga in the streets of the Jesús María neighbourhood, where rumba could be heard. He was coached on bongo and conga by Clemente Chicho Piquero and toured with bands such as the Lecuona Cuban Boys and Sonora Matancera. In 1950 he moved to New York, where he became Tito Puente's conguero and, in 1957, a member of Cal Tjader's band. He then started his own charanga and made one of the first albums of folkloric rumba and Santería music, such as Drums and Chants (1957), Mongo (1959) and Sabroso! (1959).

In the late 1950s he had his first pachanga hit, Para ti. His greatest success was his version of Herbie Hancock's Watermelon Man, which entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998 and made him a pioneer of boogaloo. He signed with Columbia, Atlantic and Fania and played in the Fania All-Stars. From the 1970s he recorded mainly salsa and Latin jazz, later for Concord Jazz and Chesky Records. He died in 2003.

Santamaría brought Afro-Cuban percussion to jazz and to the dance floor. Because he recorded for major jazz labels, his folkloric music reached many listeners. He himself said that he did not know what he was playing, he just played.
artiest/mongo-santamaria.listen: Listen to Afro Blue and notice how the congas carry the rhythm while the melody floats above the rolling accompaniment. Can you hear how jazz and Afro-Cuban percussion meet here?

artiest/monie-love.text:
Monie Love is the stage name of Simone Johnson, born Simone Gooden on 2 July 1970. She is a British rapper, actress and radio presenter. She is regarded as a pioneer among female MCs and was nominated twice for a Grammy, the first British female hip hop artist to be so.

In the late 1980s she became known through guest appearances. She rapped the woman's response on a 1989 remix of Fine Young Cannibals' She Drives Me Crazy, and appeared on United on Praise, Inner City's third album. Her debut album Down to Earth appeared in 1990, with the singles Monie in the Middle, about a woman's right to decide for herself what she wants in a relationship, and It's a Shame (My Sister), which samples a song by the Spinners that Stevie Wonder wrote. House vocalist Ultra Naté also sang on it. In 1991 she rapped on the remix of Whitney Houston's My Name Is Not Susan and appeared in the video.

In 1992 came Full-Term Love, from the film Class Act. She made her second album, In a Word or 2 (1993), with Marley Marl, and it included Born To B.R.E.E.D., a single produced by Prince. Prince also asked her to write lyrics for Carmen Electra's album. Her last single as lead artist was Slice of da Pie in 2000. Later she worked as a radio presenter in the United States, including in Philadelphia and Atlanta.
artiest/monie-love.listen: Listen to Monie in the Middle and notice how she stands up for women in her lyrics, and how loose and direct her rap sounds over the beat.

artiest/mono-blanco.text:
Mono Blanco is a Mexican group that plays son jarocho, the folk music of the Mexican state of Veracruz. The group was led by Gilberto Gutiérrez and has existed for decades. In 2017 it celebrated its fortieth anniversary at the Teatro de Bellas Artes. Its music grows out of the fandango, the village celebration where music, song and dance come together.

An important figure was Andrés Vega Delfín, nicknamed El Güero Vega, who was born in 1931 and died in 2024. In 1980 he won a competition in Tlacotalpan with his son Tereso. Gutiérrez then asked him to play the son guitar in Mono Blanco, the small guitar that carries the melody and the rhythm in this genre. Together with his sons José Tereso and Octavio he became part of the group. The Vega and Utrera families received the National Prize for Arts and Sciences for popular arts and traditions.

With the group, Vega toured many countries, including England, Spain, Morocco, India, France, Cuba, Canada, Brazil, South Africa, Australia, Germany, China, Japan and the United States several times. Mono Blanco played at festivals and worked with Mexican communities abroad. Its recordings begin with Al primer canto del gallo from 1989, followed by, among others, Fandango, Matanga and Orquesta jarocha. In this way the group kept a regional musical tradition alive and brought it to a worldwide audience.
artiest/mono-blanco.listen: Listen to a son jarocho by Mono Blanco, for example from Fandango, and notice how the stringed instruments together set up a fast, lively rhythm and how the singing moves on top of it.

artiest/monolake.text:
Monolake is a German electronic music project, founded in Berlin in 1995. It began as a duo of Gerhard Behles and Robert Henke. In 1999 Behles, Henke and Bernd Roggendorf founded the software company Ableton, and Behles turned his attention to that. In 2004 Torsten Pröfrock joined the project. Today Monolake is continued by Henke alone. The name comes from Mono Lake, a lake east of the Sierra Nevada in California.

The music is minimal techno with a dub influence. In this way Monolake helped to shape the sound of the Berlin label Chain Reaction. Later the work appeared on its own label, [ml/i]. The records have followed one another since Hongkong in 1997, including Interstate, Cinemascope, Gravity, Momentum, Polygon_Cities, Silence and Ghosts. Henke and Pröfrock also make solo work, Pröfrock under the names T++ and Various Artists.

Henke is also a software developer. He designed software and equipment for live performance, including Atlantic Waves, which allows producers in different countries to play at the same time. In 2003 he made the Monodeck, a MIDI controller that lets you edit sounds during a performance without looking at the screen. In this way Monolake became important for the way electronic music is made live, and not only for the records themselves.
artiest/monolake.listen: Listen to a track from Hongkong or Cinemascope and notice how little changes in the rhythm, and how small shifts in sound and echo still create tension.

artiest/monteverdi-choir.text:
The Monteverdi Choir is a British choir that has existed since 1964 and is counted among the most influential choirs in the world. Sir John Eliot Gardiner founded it for a performance of Claudio Monteverdi's Vespro della Beata Vergine in King's College Chapel in Cambridge. The choir is known for its stylish conviction and its wide repertoire, from the Renaissance to the twentieth century. It often performs with the English Baroque Soloists and the Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique, which Gardiner also founded.

The first recordings appeared in the 1970s and 1980s, with Music for Queen Mary, Messiah, King Arthur, Solomon, Vespro della Beata Vergine, 1610 and St. John Passion. In the year 2000, the 250th anniversary of Johann Sebastian Bach's death, the choir and the English Baroque Soloists travelled to more than sixty historic churches in Europe and a few in the United States on the Bach Cantata Pilgrimage. Almost all of Bach's church cantatas were performed and recorded there.

In 2014 the choir celebrated its fiftieth anniversary with a repeat performance of the Monteverdi Vespers from King's College Chapel, broadcast live by BBC Radio 3. In 2023 it sang at the coronation of King Charles III. In 2024 it was named best choir at the Oper! Awards in Amsterdam, and in that year Gardiner stepped down as artistic director. The choir showed how early music, with sharp, clear singing, could captivate a large audience.
artiest/monteverdi-choir.listen: Listen to a movement from the Vespro della Beata Vergine, 1610 and notice how the voices enter right after one another, so that the choir moves as a whole.

artiest/monty-norman.text:
Monty Norman was born in 1928 as Monty Noserovitch in Stepney, in London's East End, to Jewish parents. His father came from Latvia. He got his first guitar at the age of sixteen. During his national service in the RAF he became interested in singing. In the 1950s and early 1960s he sang with big bands and in variety shows, alongside comedians such as Peter Sellers and Tommy Cooper. His song False-Hearted Lover became an international success.

From the late 1950s he wrote songs for, among others, Cliff Richard, Tommy Steele, Count Basie and Bob Hope, and lyrics for musicals. He wrote the lyrics for Make Me An Offer and Expresso Bongo, which Time Out called the first rock-and-roll musical and which was filmed in 1960 with Cliff Richard. Songbook and Poppy followed later, the latter winning the prize for best musical. He also wrote film music, for example for The Day the Earth Caught Fire.

His best-known work is the James Bond Theme, which was first heard in 1962 in Dr. No. The producers were not satisfied with his arrangement, and John Barry reworked the theme. Barry later claimed that he had written it, but Norman won two libel cases, the last in 2001 against The Sunday Times. The theme is one of the best-known melodies in film history: a short, menacing melodic line that has been associated with spy films ever since. Norman died in 2022.
artiest/monty-norman.listen: Listen to James Bond Theme and notice the low, menacing guitar line with which the theme begins. Which instruments take over the melody afterwards, and how does the tension persist?

artiest/morrissey.text:
Morrissey, in full Steven Patrick Morrissey, is an English singer and lyricist, born in 1959 in Old Trafford, near Manchester, to Irish parents. He grew up in Manchester and loved literature, British social-realist films and the pop of the 1960s. In 1982 he started The Smiths with the guitarist Johnny Marr, for whom he wrote the lyrics and sang.

The debut The Smiths (1984) reached number 2 in England, Meat Is Murder (1985) number 1 and The Queen Is Dead (1986) number 2 again. The single Panic also appeared in 1986, in which Morrissey calls for the DJ to be hanged: a criticism of a radio that said nothing about the lives of his listeners. In July 1987 Marr left, and the band was already over by the time the last album, Strangeways, Here We Come, came out.

As a solo artist Morrissey began in 1988 with Viva Hate, which reached number 1 in England, with the single Suedehead. Your Arsenal (1992), Vauxhall and I (1994), You Are the Quarry (2004) and Ringleader of the Tormentors (2006) also did well. Morrissey sings with a baritone voice, and his lyrics are about loneliness, longing and resistance to authority, often with black humour and self-mockery. He is regarded as a major influence on indie pop, indie rock and Britpop. At the same time he is controversial because of his statements about immigration and national identity and his support for far-right activism.
artiest/morrissey.listen: In Panic, listen to Johnny Marr's short, cheerful guitar rhythm, which sounds like a glam rock song. Notice the ending, in which a children's choir keeps repeating the call to hang the DJ.

artiest/morten-harket.text:
Morten Harket is the singer of the Norwegian pop group a-ha. He was born in 1959 in Kongsberg and grew up in Asker, near Oslo. Before joining a-ha he sang in the soul and blues band Souldier Blue in the clubs of Oslo. In 1982 he formed a-ha with Pål Waaktaar and Magne Furuholmen, and the trio moved to London to make their breakthrough there.

Take On Me was released as early as 1984, but only became a hit in 1985, after a new recording and a video by Steve Barron. The debut album Hunting High and Low sold more than ten million copies worldwide. Scoundrel Days and Stay on These Roads, among others, followed. Harket's voice is the most recognisable element of the group: clear, with a wide range and a strong falsetto. The music magazine NME once called that falsetto the best in pop history.

After the album Memorial Beach, a-ha took a break; in 1998 the group got back together, in 2009 it stopped, and in 2015 a reunion followed. As a solo artist Harket made six albums; Wild Seed (1995) was number 1 in Norway. In 1996 he hosted the Eurovision Song Contest in Oslo. In 2012 the three members of a-ha were made knights of the Order of St. Olav. In 2025 Harket announced that he has Parkinson's disease; the treatment also affected his voice.
artiest/morten-harket.listen: In Take On Me, listen to the chorus, in which Harket climbs higher and higher to a long, high falsetto note. Notice also the fast synthesizer riff at the start, which returns between the verses.

artiest/mortimer-wilson.text:
Mortimer Wilson (1876 to 1932) was an American composer of classical music who in the 1920s also wrote music for films. He was born in Chariton, Iowa, in a rural part of the south-central part of the state. He studied organ, violin and composition in Chicago and then in Leipzig with Max Reger. After returning to the United States in 1911 he taught at the Atlanta conservatory and conducted the Atlanta Philharmonic Orchestra. In 1916 he went to Brenau College in Georgia and in 1918 to New York, where he worked as an advisory editor for the National Academy of Music until his death.

His style was late Romantic and European-influenced, comparable to that of contemporaries such as Henry Hadley and Frederick Converse. Much of his work still exists in manuscript, including five symphonies and a great deal of chamber music. The piano suite Silhouettes from the Screen of 1919 contains musical portraits of film stars such as Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks.

His best-known work for film is The Thief of Bagdad of 1924. Douglas Fairbanks encouraged him to write a full classical score, which was unusual at the time. Wilson made a leitmotif for each character and developed these symphonically. He also spent hours in the cutting room matching music and image. For Fairbanks he subsequently wrote the music for Don Q, Son of Zorro and The Black Pirate. He also wrote books, such as The Rhetoric of Music.
artiest/mortimer-wilson.listen: Listen to the music of The Thief of Bagdad and notice how each character is given a motif of their own, which returns as the story unfolds.

artiest/morton-feldman.text:
Morton Feldman was born in 1926 in Woodside, Queens, in New York, to Russian-Jewish parents. He had piano lessons and studied composition with Wallingford Riegger and Stefan Wolpe. In 1950 he heard the New York Philharmonic play Webern's Symphony and walked out in protest at the audience's indifferent reaction. In the foyer he met John Cage, with whom he became friends and went to live in the same building. Through Cage he got to know visual artists and writers, such as Jackson Pollock, Philip Guston, Robert Rauschenberg and Frank O'Hara.

With Cage's encouragement, Feldman wrote music unconnected with tonal harmony or serialism. He used notation systems of his own, often grids, which indicated how many notes sounded at a given moment, but not which ones. His experiments with notation and chance inspired Cage to pieces such as Music of Changes. Feldman was one of the most important figures of the New York School. His music is soft, slow and floating, with rhythms that seem free and sounds that remain slightly blurred. After 1977 he also wrote very long pieces.

He was inspired by abstract expressionism. In 1971 he wrote Rothko Chapel, for the building with paintings by Mark Rothko, and in 1973 For Frank O'Hara. In 1977 he wrote the opera Neither to a text by Samuel Beckett. In this way he showed that music, like painting, can limit itself to a few colours and to stillness.
artiest/morton-feldman.listen: Listen to the fifth section of Rothko Chapel and notice how little happens and how long each sound lingers. What does that silence do to your sense of time?

artiest/moscow-symphony-orchestra.text:
The Moscow Symphony Orchestra is a Russian symphony orchestra that receives no state support. The sisters Ellen and Marina Levine founded it in 1989. The musicians come from, among others, the conservatories of Moscow, Kyiv and Saint Petersburg. The current music director is the Dutch conductor Arthur Arnold, and previous music directors were Antonio de Almeida and Vladimir Ziva.

The orchestra gives its Master Series in the historic Great Hall of the Moscow Conservatory. It has played with Russian soloists such as Yuri Bashmet, Vadim Repin and Alexander Knyazev, and with international soloists such as Ana Durlovski and Torleif Thedéen. It toured most European countries and also Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, China, Argentina and the United States, and took part in festivals in Germany, Austria, Italy and Cyprus.

The orchestra's most important contribution is its recording work. It recorded more than a hundred CDs for the labels Naxos and Marco Polo, including complete series of symphonies and lesser-known work, such as Guatemala and the symphonies whose recordings appeared in the early 1990s. In this way it contributed to the familiarity of repertoire that is rarely heard outside the major concert halls. The orchestra shows how, after the Soviet era, private ensembles also emerged in Russia, which gathered musical talent from a vast area and recorded for an international market.
artiest/moscow-symphony-orchestra.listen: Listen to one of the symphonies the orchestra recorded for Naxos or Marco Polo and notice how the strings and the winds alternate in a rich, full sound.

artiest/moses-boyd.text:
Moses Boyd is a British jazz drummer, composer, producer, bandleader and radio presenter, born on 30 April 1991. He grew up in Catford in south London, the child of a Dominican father and a Jamaican mother. He began drumming at Sedgehill School. In 2016 he graduated from Trinity Laban, where he also took part in the educational jazz programme Tomorrow's Warriors.

In 2014 he formed the duo Binker & Moses with the saxophonist Binker Golding. They made three records in a row, won prizes including a MOBO Award, and released their fourth album, Feeding the Machine, in 2022. With his band Moses Boyd Exodus, in which the tuba player Theon Cross, the guitarist Artie Zaitz and the trombonist Nathaniel Cross, among others, play, he released several mixtapes in the mid-2010s. On his own label Exodus Records the EP Absolute Zero appeared in 2017, followed in 2018 by Displaced Diaspora.

His debut album Dark Matter, from 2020, was nominated for the Mercury Prize. Boyd has worked with, among others, Beyoncé, Little Simz, Lonnie Liston Smith, Sons of Kemet, Floating Points and Four Tet. In 2019 he presented a programme on BBC Radio 1Xtra. He belongs to the new generation of London jazz musicians who linked jazz with electronic music and contemporary urban music.
artiest/moses-boyd.listen: Listen to a track from Dark Matter and notice how the drums not only set the tempo but also give direction to the electronic sounds.

artiest/motley-crue.text:
Mötley Crüe is an American metal band from Hollywood, founded in 1981 by bassist Nikki Sixx and drummer Tommy Lee. Guitarist Mick Mars and singer Vince Neil soon joined. Mars came up with the name, after a remark about a motley looking crew, a ragtag-looking bunch. The umlauts were Neil's idea, reportedly inspired by the German beer the members drank.

The debut Too Fast for Love (1981) was later remixed for Elektra Records. With Shout at the Devil (1983) the band broke through in America. On Theatre of Pain (1985) the group opted for glam metal: loud guitar rock combined with make-up, backcombed hair and clothing that was sometimes androgynous. Girls, Girls, Girls (1987) entered at number 2, and Dr. Feelgood (1989) became their only studio album to reach number 1 on the Billboard 200. The band sold more than a hundred million records. The concerts were a spectacle, with guitars spitting flames and a drum kit that rode around like a roller coaster.

Behind the scenes things often went wrong. Drug addiction nearly destroyed the band in the late 1980s. Neil left in 1992 and returned in 1997. On 31 December 2015 the group gave a farewell concert in Los Angeles, but a reunion followed in 2018. The book The Dirt (2001), about their debauched life, became a bestseller and was adapted by Netflix in 2019. Together with bands such as Poison, Mötley Crüe is the textbook example of 1980s glam metal.
artiest/motley-crue.listen: In Kickstart My Heart (1989), listen to the opening, in which Mick Mars makes his guitar sound like an engine revving up. Then notice the high tempo and the shout-along chorus, typical of glam metal.

artiest/motohiko-hino.text:
Motohiko Hino (1946 to 1999), nicknamed Toko, was a Japanese jazz drummer, born in Tokyo. His father was a dancer and musician and taught him and his brother Terumasa, the later cornetist, to tap dance as children. He began drumming at the age of ten and from 1963 worked professionally, including with Hiroshi Watanabe and the Tokyo Union Orchestra.

In the 1970s he often played with his brother. He performed with his quintet at JazzFest Berlin in 1971 and at the Newport Jazz Festival in 1973. In 1971 he accompanied the singer Helen Merrill in the Gary Peacock Trio. When Terumasa left for the United States in 1975, he led trios of his own. The magazine Swing Journal repeatedly voted him Japan's best jazz drummer in the mid-1970s. His first record under his own name, First Album, appeared in 1971.

In 1978 he moved to New York. There he played with, among others, Joe Henderson, in 1979 in Hugh Masekela's band and from 1980 in JoAnne Brackeen's trio. He also worked with Sonny Rollins, John Scofield and Jean-Luc Ponty. In the 1990s two more records appeared under his own name, Sailing Stone and It's There. His drumming style was influenced by Tony Williams and Elvin Jones. He died in 1999 of cancer. His career shows how Japanese jazz passed on into the international circuit in the 1970s.
artiest/motohiko-hino.listen: Listen to a track from Sailing Stone and notice how the drums join in with the horns with plenty of movement and energy, instead of merely carrying the rhythm.

artiest/motorhead.text:
Motörhead was an English rock band, founded in London in 1975 by bassist and singer Lemmy Kilmister, guitarist Larry Wallis and drummer Lucas Fox. Kilmister wrote most of the material and was the only constant member. The best-known line-up consisted of Lemmy, drummer Phil Taylor, nicknamed Philthy Animal, and guitarist Fast Eddie Clarke. From 1992 until the end in 2015 it was Lemmy, guitarist Phil Campbell and drummer Mikkey Dee.

The band mostly played as a power trio and had several singles in the British top forty in the early 1980s. The debut album Motörhead was released in 1977. Overkill and Bomber in 1979 and Ace of Spades in 1980 established its reputation, as did the live album No Sleep 'til Hammersmith of 1981. The name Ace of Spades belongs to the best-known song, about gambling. Other themes in the lyrics were war, good and evil, abuse of power, debauchery and substance abuse.

Motörhead is regarded as a forerunner of the New Wave of British Heavy Metal, which breathed new life into the genre in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The band also influenced thrash metal and speed metal. Lemmy himself always said it was a rock 'n' roll band, which had more in common with punk bands, but with a sound of its own. In this way the group was embraced in both the punk scene and the metal scene. Lemmy died on 28 December 2015, and the next day it was confirmed that Motörhead had disbanded.
artiest/motorhead.listen: Listen to Ace of Spades and notice the racing tempo, Lemmy's raw vocals and the way the bass sounds almost like a guitar.

artiest/mr-fingers.text:
Mr. Fingers is the best-known alias of Larry Heard, born in 1960 on the South Side of Chicago. He grew up with jazz and Motown and played several instruments from an early age. At seventeen he was the drummer in the band Infinity, a jazz-fusion cover band. He worked for the American government and used that salary to buy his first studio equipment. As a drummer he felt limited, and so he bought a synthesizer and a drum machine himself.

In 1984 he bought a Roland Juno-60 and a TR-909. Within a few days he had recorded three tracks that became milestones of deep house: Can You Feel It, Mystery of Love and Washing Machine. With the singer Robert Owens and Ron Wilson he formed Fingers Inc., which in 1988 released the double album Another Side, the first full-length album in house. His singles as Mr. Fingers appeared on Trax Records and DJ International, and the compilation Ammnesia (1989) came out without his permission. Only in 1992 did his first official album, Introduction, follow.

Heard is regarded as a pioneer of deep house, which linked the futuristic outlook of house with the soft sound of disco. His 1986 single Can You Feel It had a great influence on dance music. He also recorded under other names, such as Loosefingers and Fingers Inc., and kept making music well into 2026.
artiest/mr-fingers.listen: Listen to Can You Feel It and notice the long, soft synthesizer chords above the calm rhythm. Can you hear how little the track needs to be warm and danceable all the same?

artiest/mstislav-rostropovitsj.text:
Mstislav Rostropovich (1927 to 2007) was a Soviet-Russian cellist and conductor. He was born in Baku, the son of the cellist Leopold Rostropovich, a pupil of Pablo Casals, and the pianist Sofiya Fedotova. At the age of four he had piano lessons from his mother, and at eight he began learning the cello from his father. During the Second World War the family moved to Orenburg and in 1943 to Moscow, where he entered the conservatory at sixteen.

Rostropovich was known for his interpretation and technique, but even more for his role as an inspirer of new music. He commissioned more than a hundred pieces and gave their first performances. In doing so he enriched the cello repertoire more than any cellist before or after him. He collaborated with composers such as Dmitri Shostakovich, Sergei Prokofiev, Henri Dutilleux, Witold Lutosławski, Olivier Messiaen, Luciano Berio, Alfred Schnittke and Benjamin Britten. The records from his career include the cello concertos of Dvořák, the Rococo Variations and the Symphony-Concerto for cello and orchestra.

Rostropovich was also an outspoken advocate of human rights. In 1974 he received the prize of the International League of Human Rights. He was married to the soprano Galina Vishnevskaya and received, among other honours, the Polar Music Prize. His name shows that a performer could also change classical music by prompting others to write new work.
artiest/mstislav-rostropovitsj.listen: Listen to a movement of a cello concerto that he recorded and notice how the cello sings like a human voice, with a warm, full tone.

artiest/muchatera-mujuru.text:
Muchatera Mujuru was a Zimbabwean musician from Dewedzo in Manicaland, near the border with Mozambique. He played the mbira, the traditional instrument of the Shona people, an instrument with metal tines that you play with the thumbs. In the Shona tradition he was also a medium for Chaminuka, one of the most important ancestral spirits in the Shona worldview. His music therefore belonged to ceremonies in which ancestors are invoked.

He is best known as the teacher of his grandson Ephat Mujuru (1950 to 2001), who is considered one of the best mbira players of the twentieth century. Ephat learned to play the mbira from him and gave his first ceremony at the age of ten. When Ephat's Catholic school said that playing the mbira was a sin against God, Muchatera took his grandson out of school. Ephat later learned from other masters too, Mubayiwa Bandambira and Simon Mashoko, and so followed the path of Muchatera.

Few recordings of Muchatera himself are known, and we find him mainly in the story of his grandson. He shows how in Zimbabwe the mbira was passed on from generation to generation, from grandfather to grandson, as oral knowledge and as a practice.
artiest/muchatera-mujuru.listen: Listen to a recording of mbira dzavadzimu and notice how several repeating patterns slide over one another, until you can no longer hear where one begins and the other ends.

artiest/muddy-waters.text:
Muddy Waters, born McKinley Morganfield, grew up on the Stovall Plantation near Clarksdale, Mississippi. His grandmother raised him and gave him the nickname Muddy, because he liked to play in the muddy water of Deer Creek. He first heard music in church. At seventeen he played guitar and harmonica and imitated Son House and Robert Johnson. In 1941 Alan Lomax and John W. Work III recorded him in Mississippi for the Library of Congress. In 1943 he moved to Chicago to become a musician. In 1946 he made his first records, for Columbia and then for Aristocrat Records, the young label of the Chess brothers.

In the early 1950s he recorded, with his band, with Little Walter on harmonica, Jimmy Rogers on guitar, Elgin Evans on drums and Otis Spann on piano, songs that became blues classics, sometimes with the bassist and writer Willie Dixon. They include Hoochie Coochie Man, I Just Want to Make Love to You and I'm Ready. In 1958 he travelled to England, which set off interest in the blues there. His performance at the Newport Jazz Festival in 1960 was released as his first live album.

Waters took the acoustic Delta blues to the city and gave it a sharp, electric sound with a full band. He is called the father of modern Chicago blues. His music laid the foundation for rock and roll and later rock.
artiest/muddy-waters.listen: Listen to Hoochie Coochie Man and notice the heavy voice and the stop-start rhythm of the band. Can you hear how the rhythm lingers while he sings his own myth?

artiest/muhal-richard-abrams.text: The pianist and composer Muhal Richard Abrams from Chicago taught himself his craft and played hard bop in the 1950s. In 1961 he started the Experimental Band, a group in which young musicians could try out their own work. In 1965 he co-founded the AACM with others and became its first chairman. He taught composition there and encouraged musicians to find a musical language of their own. His own work ranges from ragtime and stride to free improvisation and orchestral writing. In 1977 he moved to New York. In 2010 he received the NEA Jazz Masters award. He died in 2017.
artiest/muhal-richard-abrams.listen: Listen to how pieces from different styles are placed side by side.

artiest/muir-mathieson.text:
Muir Mathieson (1911 to 1975) was a Scottish musician who worked mainly as a music director for British film studios. He was born in Stirling into a musical family. His father was an artist and engraver, his mother a violinist, pianist and teacher, who accompanied silent films on the piano in the cinema. As a teenager he founded a youth orchestra in Stirling. In 1929 he went to the Royal College of Music in London, where he studied piano with Arthur Benjamin and conducting with Malcolm Sargent.

Sargent recommended him to the film producer Alexander Korda, whose music director he became in 1934. After the Second World War he was music director of the Rank Organisation. As music director, arranger, conductor or sometimes composer he was involved in nearly a thousand films. He himself rarely wrote the music, because he felt he lacked the talent for it. But he commissioned composers such as Arthur Bliss, Ralph Vaughan Williams, William Walton and Benjamin Britten, and helped them to fit their music precisely to the action of the film. From some scores he made concert suites.

Among the recordings associated with his name are Warsaw Concerto of 1942, The Red Shoes of 1948, Shake Hands With the Devil, Gone With the Wind and Becket. He shows how much of a film score also depends on the person who conducts, organises and brings composers together.
artiest/muir-mathieson.listen: Listen to the music of The Red Shoes and notice how the music follows the image, and what changes in the orchestra when the scene shifts in mood.

artiest/mukesh.text:
Mukesh Chand Mathur, Mukesh for short, was born in 1923 in Delhi, the sixth of ten children. His father was an engineer. He listened in on his sister's singing lessons and left school after the tenth grade. He worked briefly at the Public Works Department and meanwhile experimented with recordings of his voice. At his sister's wedding his voice caught the attention of his distant cousin, the actor Motilal, who took him to Bombay and arranged singing lessons for him. In 1941 he sang his first song, as an actor and singer, in the film Nirdosh. His first hit as a playback singer came in 1945.

At first he imitated his idol K. L. Saigal. The composer Naushad Ali helped him find a style of his own. He then sang for Dilip Kumar, until the latter chose Mohammed Rafi, and became the voice of Raj Kapoor. He sang most for the duo Shankar Jaikishan, 133 songs, followed by Kalyanji Anandji with 99. Of his four Filmfare Awards he won three for songs by Shankar Jaikishan. In 1974 he received the National Film Award for Kai Baar Yuhi Dekha Hai from Rajnigandha.

Mukesh was one of the most popular voices of Hindi cinema and was also heard as the voice of Manoj Kumar, Feroz Khan and Sunil Dutt. He died in 1976. His name belongs to the golden age of Hindi film music, in which playback singers were the voice of the screen.
artiest/mukesh.listen: Listen to Awara Hoon and notice the warm voice and the singable melody. Can you hear how clearly he lets the words come through?

artiest/mulatu-astatke.text: Mulatu Astatke was born in Jimma in Ethiopia and went to England as a teenager to study. He learned music in London and then went to Berklee in Boston. In New York he played with Latin musicians and in 1966 made Afro-Latin Soul. In the late 1960s he returned to Addis Ababa, where, amid the flourishing scene of clubs and orchestras, he developed his Ethio-jazz, with vibraphone, congas and Ethiopian scales. After the revolution of 1974 he was almost forgotten abroad. Thanks to the Éthiopiques series and the film Broken Flowers (2005) he gained a new audience. In 2009 he recorded with the British group The Heliocentrics.
artiest/mulatu-astatke.listen: Listen to the Ethiopian melody on vibraphone above a Latin rhythm.

artiest/mulgrew-miller.text:
Mulgrew Miller (1955 to 2013) was an American jazz pianist, composer and teacher. He was born in Greenwood, Mississippi, into a family without musicians, but with a piano that nobody could play. From the age of six he played songs by ear, and from the age of eight he had piano lessons. As a child he played blues and rhythm and blues at dances and gospel in churches. His great example was at first Ramsey Lewis. When, at fourteen, he saw Oscar Peterson on television, he knew he wanted to become a jazz pianist.

After his studies he played for three years in Duke Ellington's orchestra, and then accompanied the singer Betty Carter. Three years with the trumpeter Woody Shaw and three years with the Jazz Messengers of the drummer Art Blakey followed. By the end of that he was already leading groups of his own and recording under his own name, with records such as Keys to the City, Work! and Wingspan. He was then a member of Tony Williams's quintet from the beginning.

Miller developed as a hard bop player and gave it the harmonic freedom that he took from McCoy Tyner, while something of Lewis and Peterson remained in his playing. In this way he found a style of his own that influenced others from the 1980s onwards. From 2005 he headed the jazz programme at William Paterson University, and he kept performing until his death from a stroke at the age of fifty-seven.
artiest/mulgrew-miller.listen: Listen to a track from Keys to the City or Wingspan and notice how his right hand plays flowing lines, while the left hand drives the band forward with heavy chords.

artiest/mumford-en-sons.text:
Mumford & Sons is an English folk rock band from London, founded at the end of 2007 by Marcus Mumford, Ben Lovett, Ted Dwane and Winston Marshall. The name came about because Mumford was the most visible and organised the gigs. According to Lovett, it had to sound like the name of an old-fashioned family business. The band belonged to a group of young folk musicians in west London, including Laura Marling, with whom Mumford, Dwane and Marshall went on tour.

In 2008 the EP Love Your Ground appeared. The debut album Sigh No More (2009) followed, recorded with the producer Markus Dravs and paid for by the band themselves. The members did not even have instruments of their own at the time. The album includes Little Lion Man and The Cave. The sound revolves around acoustic guitar, banjo, mandolin, double bass and keyboards, with harmony vocals and a stomping bass drum. The songs often begin quietly and grow to a loud, exuberant climax. Sigh No More won a Brit Award and, after a performance with Bob Dylan at the 2011 Grammy ceremony, also attracted a great deal of attention in America.

The second album Babel (2012) entered at number 1 in the United States and won the Grammy for album of the year. In 2013 the band headlined Glastonbury. Later, on Wilder Mind (2015), the group opted for electric guitars. Mumford & Sons brought folk instruments back into the big venues and around 2010 helped to set off a wave of folk pop.
artiest/mumford-en-sons.listen: Listen to The Cave and notice the banjo and the acoustic guitar, which drive the rhythm along. Follow how the song builds to a loud climax in which the whole band and the harmony vocals come together.

artiest/munchi.text:
Munchi's real name is Rajiv Münch, and he was born in 1989 in Rotterdam, a Dutchman of Dominican descent. He began making music in 2004, when his brother gave him the program Acid Pro. In 2009 he got to know David Heartbreak through MySpace, who invited him to Charlotte after Munchi had mentioned Dave Nada's Moombahton EP. During a tour of the United States in March 2011 he suffered an attack from a brain haemorrhage. Fellow producers such as DJ Ayres, Tittsworth and Dave Nada organised a benefit for the operation and the journey home. He lay in a coma for nine hours and spent eleven days in hospital, and the support helped him recover faster.

Munchi is seen as the maker of the first truly original work within moombahton and as the inventor of moombahcore. Moombahton is a dance genre of which Dave Nada's EP was a starting point. His debut Murda Sound on T&A Records shows his versatility, with many different genres. In December 2010 three of his tracks were on M.I.A.'s mixtape Vicki Leekx, and in July 2012 he appeared with Esta Noche on Azealia Banks' mixtape Fantasea.

His music shows how a young producer from Rotterdam could break through into a worldwide dance culture via the internet and small labels, with Latin American rhythms as a basis.
artiest/munchi.listen: Listen to Sandungueo and notice the slow, heavy rhythm to which the dancers move. Can you hear which instruments carry the rhythm?

artiest/munchner-rundfunkorchester.text:
The Münchner Rundfunkorchester, in English the Munich Radio Orchestra, is a German radio orchestra in Munich. It is one of the two orchestras of the Bavarian broadcaster Bayerischer Rundfunk, alongside the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra. A predecessor already existed in the 1920s. The present orchestra took its permanent form in 1952, with Werner Schmidt-Boelke as its first chief conductor.

For a long time the emphasis was on light music, above all operettas in the early years, and the orchestra was known for its Sunday concerts. Under Lamberto Gardelli, chief conductor from 1982 to 1985, opera was added, especially Italian opera. This continued under three Italian successors: Giuseppe Patanè, Roberto Abbado and Marcello Viotti. In 2004 the broadcaster threatened to disband the orchestra. Viotti resigned in protest. After negotiations the orchestra survived, with fewer musicians, from seventy-two to fifty.

From 2006 to 2017 Ulf Schirmer was chief conductor, making recordings for the orchestra's own label BR-Klassik, including of Karl Amadeus Hartmann's Des Simplicius Simplicissimus Jugend. Ivan Repušić followed. The orchestra also recorded for CPO, RCA, Acanta and Sony Classical, with operas such as Die Entführung aus dem Serail and Hoffmanns Erzählungen, and with Carmina Burana. In this way the orchestra remained a bridge between light classical music, opera and radio.
artiest/munchner-rundfunkorchester.listen: Listen to the recording of Carmina Burana and notice how chorus and orchestra come in together sharply and powerfully, and how the rhythm drives forward.

artiest/munir-bashir.text: Munir Bashir received his first oud lessons in Mosul from his father and brother, studied at the conservatory of Baghdad and later gained his doctorate in Budapest. He was the first great oud player to give entire concerts alone, with taqsim: free improvisations in a maqam, the Arabic system of modes. He used harmonics and a tuning of his own. On his album for the French label Ocora, each piece is such a taqsim in a different maqam.
artiest/munir-bashir.listen: Listen to the taqsim in maqam Nahawand: Bashir plays short motifs, lets silences fall and so slowly builds up a melody.

artiest/munojat-yulchieva.text:
Munojat Yulchieva, in Uzbek Munojot Yoʻlchiyeva, is an Uzbek singer, born in 1960 in the Buloqboshi district in the Andijan region in the Fergana Valley. She sings classical Uzbek music and the related shashmaqom, the classical music in Persian. She is known for the distinctive colour of her voice and her natural presence. Her talent showed at an early age, and she almost became an opera singer, but the slow, aching music of her own ancient culture attracted her more strongly. Her first name means ascent to God, or simply prayer.

She performs with her mentor, the rubab player Shawqat Mirzaev, and also sings his compositions. His ensemble uses Uzbek instruments such as the dutar, a long lute with two strings, the three-stringed tanbur, the ghijak, a bowed instrument with a spike, the frame drum doira and the ney, a flute, and sometimes the chang, a zither. At concerts abroad she stands out for her traditional dress and long braids down to her waist.

In 1990 she became Meritorious Artist of the Uzbek SSR, in 1994 People's Artist of Uzbekistan, and in 1997 she won the Sharq Taronalari festival. In 2005 she performed at the Austrian festival Glatt und Verkehrt. In 2021 she received the title Hero of Uzbekistan. Her music is best known from two recordings, for the French label Ocora in 1994 and for the German Network in 1997, under the title A Haunting Voice.
artiest/munojat-yulchieva.listen: Listen to a recording of her singing with the dutar and notice how slowly her voice follows a long line, with small ornaments that sound like graceful bows.

artiest/murray-perahia.text:
Murray Perahia is an American pianist and conductor, born on 19 April 1947 in the Bronx in New York, into a family of Sephardic Jewish descent from Thessaloniki. His first language was Ladino. He began piano lessons at the age of four, but only began practising seriously at fifteen. At seventeen he studied at Mannes College with Mieczysław Horszowski. In the summers he was at the Marlboro Music Festival, where he was taught by, among others, Rudolf Serkin, Alexander Schneider and Pablo Casals. Serkin made him his assistant at the Curtis Institute.

In 1965 he won the Young Concert Artists International Auditions, and in 1972 he became the first North American to win the Leeds International Piano Competition. In 1973 he worked with Benjamin Britten and Peter Pears at the Aldeburgh Festival, of which he was co-artistic director from 1981 to 1989. In the 1980s Vladimir Horowitz, an admirer, asked him to collaborate.

Perahia is regarded as one of the greatest pianists of his time, above all as an interpreter of Bach, Handel, Scarlatti, Mozart, Beethoven and Schumann. His records include Mozart piano concertos, The Chopin Preludes and songs by Schumann. He received three Grammys and nine Gramophone Awards. His work shows how a pianist can keep the classical canon alive again and again, by listening carefully to what is in the score.
artiest/murray-perahia.listen: Listen to one of the Mozart piano concertos that he recorded, and notice how he lets the melody sing while he plays with the orchestra as a conversation partner.

artiest/muse.text:
Muse is an English rock band from Teignmouth in Devon, founded in 1994. The band consists of Matt Bellamy on vocals, guitar and keyboards, Chris Wolstenholme on bass and Dominic Howard on drums. The three played in separate school bands at Teignmouth Community College in the early 1990s. Bellamy joined Howard's band, Carnage Mayhem, as singer and songwriter, after which they renamed themselves.

The debut album Showbiz was released in 1999, with Bellamy's falsetto and a melancholy alternative rock style. Origin of Symmetry from 2001 used more instruments and romantic classical influences, and earned the band a name as an energetic live act. Absolution from 2003 added strings, as in Butterflies and Hurricanes, and was the first of seven consecutive number 1 albums in the United Kingdom. Black Holes and Revelations from 2006 contained electronic and pop elements, as in Supermassive Black Hole, and brought international success. The Resistance and The 2nd Law dealt with government oppression and popular uprising and made Muse a stadium band. Drones from 2015 was a concept album about drone warfare and reached the top of the American Billboard 200. Simulation Theory, Will of the People and The Wow! Signal followed.

Muse has won, among other awards, two Grammys and two Brit Awards, and in 2012 the Ivor Novello Award for International Achievement. The band shows how rock could blend with classical music, electronics and big themes, and thereby fill stadiums in the twenty-first century too.
artiest/muse.listen: Listen to Supermassive Black Hole and notice how electronic sounds and guitar together set up a tight, danceable rhythm, with Bellamy's high voice above it.

artiest/music-department-of-the-imperial.text:
The music department of the Japanese Imperial Household Agency takes care of Japan's court music, called gagaku. The Imperial Household Agency is a government body that manages the affairs of the imperial family. The institution goes back to institutions from the Taihō codes of 701 and 702 and, until the Second World War, was called the Ministry of the Imperial Household. Its headquarters stands on the grounds of the Imperial Palace in Tokyo. Within that institution, court musicians preserve a tradition that is centuries old.

Gagaku is Japan's oldest court music. An orchestra of wind instruments, string instruments and percussion plays slow, solemn pieces, in which the music changes slowly and long sounds are given plenty of room. A well-known piece is Etenraku, which appears in School of Rock in the mode Hyōjō. The musicians play instruments such as the sho, a mouth organ, the hichiriki, a double-reed flute, and the ryūteki, a transverse flute.

The influence reaches beyond Japan. The Japanese composer Toru Takemitsu wrote In an Autumn Garden for gagaku orchestra in 1979, in which he combined the traditional sound with a contemporary composition. In this way the music department shows how a court music could be maintained without interruption and yet inspire new compositions.
artiest/music-department-of-the-imperial.listen: Listen to Etenraku. Notice the long, sustained sounds of the mouth organ and the high, piercing double-reed flute, and how slowly the piece unfolds.

artiest/musica-antiqua-koln.text:
Musica Antiqua Köln was a German early music ensemble, founded in 1973 by Reinhard Goebel and fellow students from the conservatory in Cologne. The ensemble devoted itself mainly to music of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, played according to the performance practice of the time. After more than thirty years of tours, recordings and concerts the group was disbanded in 2007. Goebel then focused on conducting larger orchestras, in both early and modern repertoire.

The group made many recordings for the label Archiv Produktion, which belongs to Deutsche Grammophon, and received numerous awards, including the Grand Prix International du Disque, the Gramophone Award and the Diapason d'Or, as well as Grammy nominations. The records include Bach's Das Musikalische Opfer BWV 1079 and Die Kunst der Fuge BWV 1080, Handel's Wassermusik, Flötenkonzerte and Deutsche Kammermusik vor Bach, and also Monteverdi's Il Combattimento di Tancredi e Clorinda. The group made its last recording for Archiv, Telemann's Flute Quartets of 2005, with the recorder player Maurice Steger.

Many people know the ensemble from the soundtrack of the film Le Roi Danse, about the life and music of the court composer Jean-Baptiste Lully. In this way the group brought to life Baroque music, which to the general public sometimes seemed dusty, with a sharp, lively sound.
artiest/musica-antiqua-koln.listen: Listen to a movement from Die Kunst der Fuge BWV 1080 and notice how different voices take up the same theme one after another and keep an eye on one another.

artiest/muthuswami-dikshitar.text:
Muthuswami Dikshitar (1776 to 1835) was a South Indian poet, singer, veena player and composer of classical Indian music. He was born in Tiruvarur near Thanjavur, in present-day Tamil Nadu, into a Tamil Brahmin family. He had two brothers, Chinnaswami and Balaswami, and a sister, Balamba. He was the youngest member of the Trinity of Carnatic music, alongside Tyagaraja and Syama Sastri.

Dikshitar wrote about five hundred compositions. They are known for their extensive poetic descriptions of Hindu gods and detailed imagery of temples. In all his compositions he used the signature Guruguha, in the form of a mudra. Unlike Tyagaraja and Syama Sastri, who wrote mainly in Telugu, he wrote mostly in Sanskrit. A few kritis he made in Manipravalam, a literary style that combines Sanskrit and Tamil.

His music captures the essence of a raga in the style of the veena, in which gamakas, the bends and ornaments of a note, are central. His pieces are mostly in a slow tempo, the chowka kala, with occasional verses at medium tempo. They are still widely performed in Carnatic concerts. He shows how in the South Indian tradition music, poetry and religion flow into one another, and how a composer can still be heard in the concert hall almost two centuries after his death.
artiest/muthuswami-dikshitar.listen: Listen to a composition by Dikshitar on the veena or in a vocal performance and notice how slowly the melody unfolds, with bending notes that give the raga a face of its own.

artiest/my-bloody-valentine.text:
My Bloody Valentine is an Irish rock band, founded in Dublin in 1983 by the singer and guitarist Kevin Shields and the drummer Colm Ó Cíosóig. After many changes, the bassist Debbie Googe joined in 1985 and the singer and guitarist Bilinda Butcher in 1987. The name comes from the 1981 horror film My Bloody Valentine, a title that Shields says he did not know when it was suggested to him. The first years were difficult, with records that had little success.

In 1988 the band signed with Creation Records. Several EPs and the album Isn't Anything (1988) appeared there. The next album, Loveless (1991), is regarded as their masterpiece and a milestone of shoegaze. The label dropped the band because of the high production costs. In 1992 it signed with Island Records and recorded a great deal of material, but remained largely inactive. In 1997 the band broke up. In 2007 it got back together for a world tour, and in 2013 the third album, m b v, followed, which received much praise.

The band's sound is characterised by distorted guitars, subdued androgynous vocals and unusual production techniques. The vocals often disappear into the guitar sounds, so that the music sounds more like a floating whole than like a song with a clear foreground. In this way they became pioneers of shoegaze.
artiest/my-bloody-valentine.listen: Listen to Only Shallow and notice how guitar and vocals merge. Can you still follow the singing voice, or does it sound like an extra guitar in the wall of sound?

artiest/my-chemical-romance.text:
My Chemical Romance is an American rock band from New Jersey. The singer Gerard Way and the drummer Matt Pelissier founded it in September 2001, shortly after the attacks of 11 September, which influenced Way in his decision to start a band. The guitarist Ray Toro, the bassist Mikey Way and later the guitarist Frank Iero joined. The name comes from a book title by Irvine Welsh, which Mikey saw in a bookshop. The debut I Brought You My Bullets, You Brought Me Your Love was released in 2002 on Eyeball Records.

The band then signed with Reprise Records and in 2004 released Three Cheers for Sweet Revenge, with Helena. Shortly after its release Pelissier was replaced by Bob Bryar. The album was a commercial success. Even bigger was The Black Parade (2006), a rock opera as a concept album, with the single Welcome to the Black Parade topping the British chart. In 2010 Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys followed. In 2013 the band split up, but in 2019 it got back together, with a tour in 2022 and 2023.

The music combines pop punk, hard rock and theatrical arrangements. The band is counted as emo, a label that it rejects itself. It is seen as one of the most influential rock groups of the 2000s, with a loyal and young audience.
artiest/my-chemical-romance.listen: Listen to Helena and notice how Gerard Way's singing alternates between restrained and screaming. Can you hear how the guitars heighten the drama of the song?

artiest/myllarguten.text:
Myllarguten, which means the Miller's Boy, is the nickname of Torgeir Augundsson (1801 to 1872), one of the best-known Norwegian folk musicians, around whom many stories have arisen. He was born in Sauherad in Telemark. The precise year of his birth is disputed, and the entries in the church registers are unclear about his background. His father Augund was a village fiddler and worked at the local mill. That is where the son got his name.

According to the story, Torgeir did not dare to play the fiddle for fear of his father. He did it in secret while his father was at work. One day his father came home early, heard someone playing and asked in amazement who it was. His wife Gunhild had to admit that it was their son. After that Augund taught him, but the boy was so eager that he had to send him to other players in the area. His teachers included Knut Lurås, Jon Kjos, Mattis Flathus and Øystein Langedrag, a former soldier from the Napoleonic wars whose military music also influenced Myllarguten's style.

As his name grew, Torgeir became a harsh critic and a ruthless competitor, who could not bear being outdone. Only Håvard Gibøen, his counterpart from Telemark, he called the master of them all. To this day Myllarguten is regarded as the yardstick in Norwegian folk music.
artiest/myllarguten.listen: Listen to a recording of a Norwegian folk fiddle from Telemark and notice how the melody is played with sharp, almost dancing bow strokes.
